did_you_know.text: Did you know? Timnah was the place where Samson saw a Philistine woman and asked to marry her, even though his parents objected.
Did you know? According to the text, choosing the Philistine woman was part of a process that the Lord used to create a confrontation with the Philistines, who ruled over Israel at that time.
Did you know? Samson tore the young lion apart with his bare hands, and the text attributes his strength in that act to the Spirit of the Lord, which came powerfully upon him.
Did you know? Some time later, Samson found a swarm of bees and honey inside the carcass of the lion he had killed—an unusual sight that later became the basis for his riddle.
Did you know? Samson ate some of the honey and even gave some to his parents, but he did not tell them that he had found it inside the lion’s carcass.
Did you know? When Samson arrived to marry the woman, he held a feast, and the text notes that this was a customary practice among young men.
Did you know? The local men provided Samson with thirty companions, or attendants, during the feast.
Did you know? Samson’s riddle was based on a contrast: “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.” The answer referred to the lion and the honey.
Did you know? Samson’s companions threatened to burn his wife and her father’s household in order to pressure her to obtain the answer to the riddle during the seven days of the feast.
Did you know? After learning that the townsmen had solved the riddle through his wife, Samson went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty men, and gave their garments to those who had solved the riddle.
